Pia comes to her therapy session late. First, Pia goes to the bathroom to wash her hands and face. She carries with her a very heavy backpack. She sits down, wipes her forehead, scratches her arms, takes her water bottle out of her backpack, and then puts the water bottle back in the backpack after she chugs some water. Often, she asks for air conditioning to be put on. She just cannot get settled. Also, she sweats profusely and wipes her face, and her shirt often is drenched from sweat.

All of these behaviors were worse in this session. In addition, the noise connected to all of these activities that she needs to perform in order to get settled in, bothered me more than ever before. In the past, I had noted my observations to her regarding how it takes a long time for her to settle in, and that there are many steps that she needs to take in order to get more comfortable. However, I was unable in the past to bring to her attention another aspect of these rituals. That is, the hostility that was so palpable. In this session, I was able to let her know that she started the session trying to get settled, kind of like a baby that needed to be swaddled, contained and comforted all at the same time. Furthermore, I was able to now add her hostility to my interpretation by letting her know that all of the noise and motion kept me from being able to think. As soon as I pointed out both of these aspects, my patient stopped moving and became quiet for the rest of the session. That is, she could begin to focus on the work of the therapy session and not feel bothered, and at the same time not bother me. We were both finally comfortable.

I felt very proud of my ability to point out these observations to Pia. I thought of Joe Lichtenberg right then and there. I had this visual image of Joe sitting next to me and that we were smiling at each other in the same moment I was able to let my patient know about some disruptions in her infancy that she carried forward to this day. I thought Joe would be proud of me, and that I now understood his passionate commitment to being able to go back into the infancy of his patients in order to understand what was present in the here and now.

A funny thing happened as I was writing this coda after being immersed in the three issues of Psychoanalytic Inquiry devoted to Joe Lichtenberg Remembered. I turned to my side and Joe was sitting next to me, supporting and creating as always which I realized had energized what I was doing with ideas for many years. We were working together as we had many times before. It was as if we were still trying to bring coherence out of a plethora of partially formed ideas that characterize psychoanalysis.

The ideas were exciting but did not fit completely well together and together did not adequately focus on the importance of the depth or size of the present moment in real living time. This last paper of Joe’s is a major contribution to improving our understanding of how a sense of power is an essential issue to be explored in the real-time relationship between the patient and the analyst in the clinical hour.

As we sat there, side by side, we agreed that using many of the insights and ideas within psychoanalysis would lead to an improved understanding of the connection between hope and a sense of power in the analyst and patient; and, how they function to transform suffering into love and joy. While the past is really the past, it is a gift to help us grow and embrace life as it is. Exploration of these ideas is becoming the essence of this monograph.

During the time that Joe was writing “A Sense of Power,” he and I spoke about it almost daily. I was his sounding board. He read me sentences and paragraphs, wanting to make sure that he was communicating clearly the meaning he ascribed to this concept, a sense of power. He was determined to elaborate both a theory of a sense of power, and its application to the psychoanalytic process. He intended his work on power to be an elaboration of his previous work on motivational systems, narrative, and the nature of the clinical exchange between patient and therapist. In those formulations he spelled out “seeking” as the crucial source of motivation. As Joe said, “all creatures are born with some capacity to seek to discover what they need and want and to seek to obtain it, removing obstacles if necessary. Humans add to the motivational systems involved in successfully seeking a recognition of the meaning of their seeking to their own welfare and the welfare of others … in the absence of what they seek they can imagine – that is, create a fantasy – an illusion of the desired … … When dealing with an actuality, success in its attainment leads to pride [a sense of power] and an incentive to seek for the success, and failure results in disappointment and an incentive to modify and review the effort … Disruption of a broadly maintained illusion is often traumatic, leading to feels of disillusion … [a drop in the sense of power] … and deep feelings of pessimism, helplessness, confusion, shame, and a loss of vitality” (An Experience-Based Vision of Psychoanalytic Theory and Practice, Chapter 4, p. 109). Thus for Joe, the contribution of the concept of a “sense of power” was both a refinement of theory and a rethinking of the therapeutic relationship between analyst and patient.

Already apparent in Joe’s published papers and books and those published in collaboration with his colleagues, is his conceptual refinement of “a sense of power.” His early concepts of “a doer doing,” and “seeking” already contain both the effort involved and the richness contained in actualizing the sense of power. “a doer doing,” and “seeking” reflect an individual’s inborn sense of agency. Conversely, this sense of agency is the impetus for a doer doing, and seeking. One might well say, “I seek therefore I am,” as well as, “I am therefore I seek.” A sense of power is also inherent in motivational systems such as “mastery of the environment” and “regulation of physiological requirements.” These motivations require an assertion of specific actions initiated by the doer.

The psychoanalytic exchange is a highly complex, nuanced, and difficult to master process. This paper employs Lichtenberg’s formulation of a personal sense of power to address often befuddling exchanges that can occur between analyst and difficult-to-treat patients. A sense of power provides self-regulatory as well as interactive regulatory functions for each participant. One’s sense of agency lies at the heart of such a sense of power. Recognizing fluctuations in the analyst’s sense of power and in the patient’s sense of power can inform the treatment situation. I demonstrate how these formulations can suggest a more impactful, therapeutic, affective engagement between analyst and patient. Several clinical examples explore how challenging therapeutic situations such as eruptive aggression, entrenched depression, racism, and misogyny can be approached in new ways. The elaborated approach can facilitate significant transformations for patients, and a greater sense of competence and satisfaction for the treating analyst.

The dream functions dynamically to organize data, to reinforce memory, to resolve conflict, and to perform many of the cognitive functions of what we refer to as waking thinking during REM and NREM brain periods that occur at night. Our understanding is informed by an understanding of sleep physiology and cognitive psychology, which introduce powerful changes in contemporary psychoanalytic theory, especially the research-based conceptualization of the implicit and explicit domains of learning, memory and knowledge, and by developments in the psychophysiology of sleep and dreaming, dream-content research and neuroscience. Rather than “lost on the royal road,” perhaps paradoxically during these constructivist times, we know more about dreaming and its functions than ever before. Dreams can no longer be viewed as a royal road to the unconscious, but as a royal road to unconscious thinking. I have named this model as the organizational model of dreams.

Joe Lichtenberg had a passion for exploring and elaborating the human condition. That passion was something we shared. This monograph honors our commitment to that exploration and its clinical implications that we dialogued about before he died.

I will never forget that Sunday morning around 10AM when he called. He said, “Arthur, I have an idea I know you will understand. It is a personal sense of power.” This is how this monograph was born. We confirmed that he did not mean a sense of power over another. We elaborated that we meant a sense of power as a motivating process influencing the organization and expression of one’s sense of self. We spoke for about 45 minutes. Joe talked of agency, affect, intentions, and goals. The sense of power resulted from an agentic assertion realized or unrealized. Realized, that assertion resulted in a sense of power. Unrealized, there would be a loss of that sense. We shared that the sense of power would wax or wane according to whether one’s intention could be realized or were thwarted. My emphasis was that the stability of a sense of power reflected the stability of one’s sense of cohesiveness, coherence. An unstable waxing and waning of a personal sense of power reflected an unstable sense of self. A stable sense of power is maintained even in states of frustrated intentions.

Joe preferred to emphasize the frustration model. We then talked about successful and unsuccessful ways of restoring a loss of power. Again, I sustained the notion that restoring a loss of power was more or less successful depending on the stability of the sense of self. With our excited exploration, Joe promised to send me a draft of his ideas. He wished to have me contribute to the monograph.

As Joe was writing out his conceptualization of a personal sense of power, Mady Chalk was there as “his sounding board” (Prologue, this issue, p. 789). She shared in, encouraged, and challenged his evolving formulations. Joe explored his developing ideas with Elizabeth Carr and a group at ICP+P in Washington, DC. Elizabeth, learning of my engagement with Joe in these formulations, invited my paper on “Diversity, Power, and Affective Engagement.” And, of course, Joe’s long-time collaborators Frank Lachmann and Jim Fosshage contributed their papers.

Introduction from Mei-Fun Kuang, Ph.D

I was very excited to come to this project, a ground-breaking issue of Psychoanalytic Inquiry that focuses exclusively on the voices of mainland Chinese therapists/analysts and their patients. Although I am a native of Taiwan, my parents are originally from mainland China and are descendants from the Xibo ethnic minority group as well as from the Han people. I also lived and worked in Japan for several years and speak Japanese fluently. I met my co-editor, Hawlan Ng, when we worked together for a U.S.-based multinational consulting firm. Although I am Chinese (and my patients are primarily in mainland China), I am well-versed in navigating different cultures and subcultures. I was certified as a Jungian analyst by the International Association of Analytical Psychology (IAAP).

Soon it will be the 100-year anniversary of Psychology recognized as an official academic discipline in China since the Academia Sinica Institute of Psychology was established in 1928. Psychology, translated into Xin Li in Chinese, which means Heart (Mind) Science, has grown from a Western concept into one of the most discussed topics in current Chinese people’s daily lives. In the past twenty years, many Western psychologists and analysts have come to China to teach psychology, and the practices of psychological counseling, psychoanalysis and analytical psychology have begun to take firm root in Chinese society. Being in analysis is increasingly seen as an important step toward becoming a psychologist and toward individuation. Not only have many Chinese people undergone analysis, but there are now many Chinese psychologists trained and currently working as professional analysts. Psychoanalysis has its origins in the West but had to evolve in new ways to accommodate a Chinese psyche embedded in Chinese culture, which itself has changed a great deal in recent years.

We are in the second century of the information age, everywhere confronted by information’s shadow, which serves our desires only by shaping what we know and what we want others to know. In this age of shadow, the ego enlarges to impose its will over human history. However, a bigger ego casts a larger shadow.

In the Teachers’ Lounge: Creating a Community Space for Psychoanalytic Teachers

Mark Moore PHD

Mark Moore

2400 Chestnut Street, Suite 2810, Philadelphia, PA 19103
markmoorephd@icloud.com

Mark Moore   Clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst who works in private practice in Philadelphia. He was the Director of Psychological Services at the Abramson Cancer Center at Pennsylvania Hospital from 2004–2014. He was also the Director of the Psychotherapy Training Program from 2014–2020 at the Psychoanalytic Center of Philadelphia, where he is a faculty member and teacher. He currently teaches two courses on Writing, and a comparative course on Psychotherapy and Psychoanalysis, and runs a Balint group for students. He has written on a range of topics including the concept of harmony in Japan; cultural perspectives on lying; conducting therapy outside the office; the experience of bodily betrayal in illness and aging; shame across the adult lifespan; and the psychological significance of friendship. In 2020, he received the Edith Sabshin Teaching Award from the American Psychoanalytic Association.
Psychoanalytic teaching, support, andragogy, frame, idealization, classroom process

The author describes how a teaching forum was started at his local institute, with the goal of helping to support and sustain faculty in their work as psychoanalytic teachers. Psychoanalytic teachers receive little training or mentorship, and there are few opportunities to discuss their classroom experiences, despite the challenges of shifting from the dyadic experience of the therapist’s office to the group dynamics of the classroom. The author discusses various challenges for psychoanalytic teachers in making that transition, while also considering how our awareness of the frame, the risks of idealization and transference can aid us as teachers. An example of a forum meeting about the use of assigned readings demonstrates how a focus on the process of reading can be a more effective form of teaching foundational psychoanalytic concepts than simply teaching content or concepts from papers.

ASK ME! A Visit to the Rijksmuseum or the Analyst As a Painter

Giuseppe Civitarese PHD MD

Giuseppe Civitarese

1 Piazza A. Botta, Pavia 27100, Italy
gcivitarese@gmail.com
http://orcid.org/0000-0002-3466-4329

Giuseppe Civitarese   Psychiatrist and training and supervising analyst of the Italian Psychoanalytic Society (SPI), and a member of the American Psychoanalytic Association (APsaA) and of the International Psychoanalytic Association (IPA). He lives and is in private practice, in Pavia, Italy. His most recent books include Sublime Subjects: Aesthetic Experience and Intersubjectivity in Psychoanalysis, London 2018; Vitality and Play in Psychoanalysis (with A. Ferro), Milan 2022; Psychoanalytic Field Theory: A Contemporary Introduction, London 2022; The Hour of Birth: Psychoanalysis of the Sublime and Contemporary Art, London 2023, in press; On Arrogance: A Psychoanalytic Essay, London 2023, in press. In 2022, he received the Sigourney Award.
Aura, distance, intercorporeity, Vermeer, Rijksmuseum, sublime, mise en abîme

The article is actually made up of a series of digressions representing the author’s unique approach to engaging with J. Palmer’s ideas and offering a response. Instead of constituting a formal discussion, they have evolved into marginal notes inspired by an occasional visit to Amsterdam’s Rijksmuseum, which is world famous for the masterpieces it houses. This formula allows for the exploration of various issues related to representation in art and life, as inherently intersubjective. The problems of aesthetic experience overlap with those of psychoanalysis, and vice versa: themes such as distance and aura; the relationship between content and container, i.e., between form and content or between frame and artistic motif; the aesthetics of the sublime as a portrayal of the vicissitudes of the primary relationship with the object; the negative of the invisible as what enables vision; art as a thematization of intersubjectivity; the artistic gesture as the movement and expression of the body, or rather, of intercorporeality; the construction of meaning that occurs in the “carnal” intimacy with art; painting as meditation on perception as unconscious (Merleau-Ponty); the pictorial structure of the dream within the dream or mise en abîme: these are all themes touched upon in a fragmented manner but that refer to various other works in which the author has addressed them, giving the sense of an ongoing research endeavor, where what matters is not the destination but the process of traversing the path of art as access to the psyche. All are interwoven in a series of internal references, the final figure or figures of which are left substantially open. The importance of reflection on art in general is continually reaffirmed in the work, both explicitly and implicitly, in the lines and between the lines.
